planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Alabama Blue is a cold-hardy heirloom collard whose flavor sweetens noticeably after frost.

directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or transplant to final spacing once seedlings have several true leaves. Alabama Blue is a Deep South heirloom collard grown for generations for its striking blue-green, slightly savoyed leaves and excellent cold hardiness, surviving hard freezes that damage less hardy greens and developing sweeter, milder flavor after exposure to frost. The tall, upright plants produce abundant leaves over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again style, taking outer leaves as needed while the center continues producing. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best leaf production, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, which can be managed with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide.

common_name: Green Glaze Collard (Waxy Insect-Resistant Heirloom Collard)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Green Glaze's thick, waxy cuticle deters cabbage worms and other leaf-chewing pests better than most collard varieties.

directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard, prized among organic growers for its thick, glossy, cabbage-like leaf surface that gives noticeably better natural resistance to cabbage worms, loopers, and flea beetles than standard collard varieties, reducing the need for pest control sprays. The tall, vigorous plants produce large, tender leaves with good flavor over a long cut-and-come-again harvest season, and cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, as with other collards. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season, and although the glossy leaves offer real pest resistance, monitor young transplants closely, since seedlings are more vulnerable before the waxy cuticle fully develops.

common_name: Yellow Cabbage Collard (Virginia Heading Heirloom Collard)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring; unlike open, loose-leaf collards, Yellow Cabbage Collard forms a loose head, so give it slightly more room and a longer season to fully develop.

directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants ample room to form their characteristic loose head. Yellow Cabbage Collard is a distinctive Virginia heirloom, unusual among collards for forming a semi-blanched, cabbage-like heart of pale yellow-green leaves at the plant's center rather than staying fully open-leaved, giving it a milder, sweeter flavor and more tender texture than typical collards, especially in the blanched inner leaves. Outer leaves can still be harvested cut-and-come-again style through the season, while the forming head is left to mature for a more tender harvest later. Cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, and the plant tolerates hard freezes well. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best head development.
